Where the project began

Last semester’s
course project

Event Driven and Process Oriented Architectures

We developed FT-Engrave, an event-driven system for a FischerTechnik factory.

The application coordinated orders for customised AirTags through engraving, polishing, and quality control.

github.com/sejmasijaric/edpo-project

Course name and last-semester context supplied by the project author. The repository describes FT-Engrave as an event-driven factory control system for customised AirTags, with intake, manufacturing, and quality-control stages. Its architecture includes workflow services and machine integration over HTTP with MQTT telemetry. Source: https://github.com/sejmasijaric/edpo-project/blob/main/README.md . The original motivation

Development away from the factory

We “vibe coded” the simulator so we would not have to visit the factory every time we worked on the project.

A tool for the course project

We built it quickly with AI to support our development workflow.

A local substitute for the hardware

It supplied HTTP machine endpoints, MQTT telemetry, and a web interface for interacting with simulated items.

The immediate goal was to keep developing and testing the application without physical access.

The project author describes the original simulator as completely vibe coded and created to avoid travelling to the factory for every development session. This is the team's account of how and why it was built. We are not inferring that AI-generated code necessarily lacks architecture or tests. Existing simulator features are documented at https://github.com/sejmasijaric/edpo-project/blob/main/factory-simulator/README.md . The main repository documents a simulation deployment that replaces the factory and MQTT broker locally.

Project objective

What we intend to deliver

01A migrated simulator

Preserve the FischerTechnik functionality and required HTTP/MQTT behaviour.

02A reusable Java foundation

Separate shared state, transfers, and timing from factory-specific behaviour.

03A second factory layout

Run a complete route with two manipulators and a conveyor.

04Evidence and documentation

Provide regression tests, extension tasks, and reproducible demonstrations.

Source: root design.md, Goal and reference layouts; scope-proposal.md, Proposed outcome. We will establish the exact compatibility requirements before migration. The intended contribution is a reusable foundation supported by evidence from two layouts.

Implementation plan

Migration and the second layout

01Migrate in small increments

Move the remaining FischerTechnik behaviour and rerun the relevant baseline cases.

02Build the transfer route

Input, first manipulator, conveyor, second manipulator, output.

03Reuse existing functions

Use shared state, timing, and transfer handling. Reuse machine behaviour where it fits.

04Record design changes

Document factory-specific code, duplication, and any core changes the second layout needs.

Output: two runnable demonstrations using the same shared foundation.

Source: root design.md, Migration and implementation sequence. We will assemble a small part of the second factory early, then complete its route after the main migration. The goal is meaningful reuse, not a promise of zero core edits. A representative second layout demonstrates reuse between factory models, not support for arbitrary laboratory systems.

Implementation plan

Shared timing interface

Runtime behaviour

A three-second action takes approximately three real seconds.

Command receipt starts the action. The machine stays busy until the scheduled completion.

Implementation approach

We will use standard Java scheduling behind a shared abstraction.

Fast, controlled tests

Tests will replace the scheduler and trigger pending completions directly.

Reset or failure must invalidate an obsolete completion so it cannot later move a workpiece.

Source: root design.md, Initial timing decision. This is ordinary real-time pacing, without a hard real-time guarantee. Integration checks need an agreed tolerance. Tests can advance completion using a helper without adding an accelerated production clock. We will define command handling while busy and ensure state changes occur in a controlled order. A cancellation handle or action-generation check is a candidate implementation detail to choose during extraction.

Implementation plan

Explicit fault scenarios

ScenarioWhat we will changeExpected check
Normal operationNo injected fault.The route completes with the expected final state.
Longer durationIncrease one action duration.The machine remains busy until completion.
Machine failureFail a selected action before transfer.The workpiece stays in a valid location.
Telemetry suppressionSuppress selected outgoing messages for an interval.Only selected messages stop. Publishing resumes after clearing.

Each scenario will define its trigger, expected response, and clear or reset behaviour.

Source: root design.md, Scenarios. Use fixed durations and explicit triggers such as an action number or elapsed time from scenario start. Suppression applies to selected outgoing telemetry, not arbitrary network failure. Unless the model specifies otherwise, message suppression does not stop internal machine execution. We will define what resuming publication means and will not assume replay of suppressed messages. Reset tests must reject obsolete scheduled completions.

Evaluation plan

Evaluation questions and evidence

QuestionEvidence we will collect
CompatibilityBefore-and-after baseline results and HTTP/MQTT contract checks.
CorrectnessState and transfer assertions across normal, delayed, failed, and reset cases.
ReuseA component map for both layouts and a record of duplicated or specialised code.
Maintainability and extensionChange records for a duration edit, a new machine instance, and a route change.

We will agree the acceptance cases before implementation and report failures as well as successes.

Source: root design.md, Evaluation. The following slides operationalise these questions as a proposed evaluation protocol. These are planned methods, not measured results or accepted numeric thresholds. The report will connect each claim to a test, demonstration, or documented code change.
